subject: Cloud Computing
title: The Digital Divide
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Digital Divide usable.

hook.text: Cloud services need fast internet. But 2.6 billion people still lack reliable connectivity.

buildup.text: In wealthy nations, the cloud powers everything. Elsewhere, basic internet is still a dream.

discovery.text: Projects like Starlink aim to bring internet to remote areas via low-orbit satellites.

twist.text: Even where internet exists, cloud services priced in dollars are unaffordable in many places.

climax.text: The cloud revolution is real, but it hasn't reached everyone. Access remains deeply unequal.

punchline.text: The cloud works everywhere. The internet doesn't.

quiz.question: What is the main barrier to global cloud adoption?
options: Billions of people still lack reliable and affordable internet access
Cloud computing only works in cold climates
Most countries have banned cloud services for security reasons

details.summary: Cloud computing requires reliable internet access, creating a digital divide between connected and unconnected regions. While cloud enables developing nations to access infrastructure without building data centers, over two billion people still lack reliable internet access.
details.whyItMatters: The cloud's benefits are not equally distributed globally. The digital divide means that cloud's democratizing potential remains unrealized for billions of people.
takeaways: Cloud requires reliable internet that billions lack
Developing nations can leapfrog infrastructure via cloud
Mobile-first cloud access is bridging some gaps

faq.question: How does cloud help developing nations?
faq.answer: Cloud eliminates the need to build local data centers and IT infrastructure. A startup in Nairobi can access the same computing power as one in San Francisco. Mobile payment systems like M-Pesa demonstrate how cloud services can leapfrog traditional infrastructure limitations.

faq.question: What is being done about the digital divide?
faq.answer: Initiatives like Starlink, Project Loon, and undersea cable investments aim to extend internet access globally. Cloud providers are opening regions in underserved areas. Mobile-first strategies and edge computing can reduce bandwidth requirements for cloud access.
